transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Nakamura. I wanted to come by and talk to you about the imaging you had earlier today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is everything okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, there was a bit of a situation with the procedure. Some things didn't go quite right with the administration of the contrast dye.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We had an issue with the protocol. The contrast was given, but your lab results showed your kidneys were already under some stress.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I saw my creatinine was high on the portal. Does that mean my kidneys are failing now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry for any confusion here, but it was just a very busy morning in the radiology suite and the check wasn't performed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm reading here that contrast can cause acute kidney injury. Is that what happened?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But the main thing is that we are monitoring your output now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like I can't really breathe right now. My chest feels tight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We just need to look at the current numbers. I'm looking at your chart right now and the levels are stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've never been in a hospital before. I don't know how to do this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a common feeling.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Did you ignore the lab results?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was some confusion with the chart review process. I'm sorry that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is the damage permanent?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We don't know that yet. But for now, the plan is to start you on intravenous fluids immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do the fluids do?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: They help flush the dye out of your system. I'll have the nurse start the IV bag in the next ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I have to do anything?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your only role right now is to let us know if you feel any new pain or if you notice you aren't urinating as much.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll keep track of it on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That works. I'll come back and check your blood work tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to see where the levels are.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Do you have any other questions about the IV?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Alright, I'll let the nurse know.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language ('But the main thing is...') to redirect the patient during a moment of distress regarding breathing and chest tightness.

E.justification: The resident uses platitudes ('things didn't go quite right', 'some confusion') and never explicitly names the error (failure to check creatinine/labs before contrast).

A.justification: Direct apologies are offered, but they are diluted by excuses regarding a 'very busy morning' and 'confusion with the chart review process'.

R.justification: The resident uses generic validation ('I understand', 'It is a common feeling') and meets the patient's physical/emotional distress with factual redirection to the chart.

T.justification: Resident provides specific steps (IV fluids, blood work), timelines (10 minutes, tomorrow at 8 AM), a named patient role (monitoring output), and a prevention/mitigation strategy (flushing the dye).
